title: The grocer's parrot
hookLine: a parrot spills oil, is struck bald, and decides every bald man must have spilled oil too (Masnavi 1.247ff)

lines: THEY MUST FEEL WHAT I'D FEEL.
cards: You see someone crying in a parking lot and think: breakup, I've been there. A coworker is quiet in a meeting and you think: they're mad; I get quiet when I'm mad.

It happens all day: assuming what's inside someone else is what would be inside you, usually without noticing. Rumi's second story in the Masnavi is short, funny, a little sharp, and about exactly this. It stars a bird.

teach.h: A TALKING PARROT SPILLS THE OIL.
teach.b: A grocer had a parrot, green and clever, that chatted with the customers and kept an eye on the shop. One day, while the grocer was out, a cat dashed after a mouse.
The parrot panicked, flapped across the counter, and knocked over the bottles of rose oil. Oil everywhere.
The grocer came back, saw the mess, and in his anger struck the parrot on the head. Its head feathers fell out. It was bald, and it stopped talking.
The grocer was heartbroken. He sighed, pulled at his beard, and gave money to the poor, hoping his parrot would speak again. Days went by in silence.
Then a wandering dervish walked past the shop, his head completely shaved, bald and shining. And the parrot suddenly found its voice: hey, you! How did you end up bald?
Did you spill oil from a bottle too? Everyone laughed. The parrot had made a comparison, a qiyas, and it was wrong.
Same bald head, entirely different story. Here Rumi turns: don't measure the deeds of the holy by yourself. He adds a Persian pun.
Sher and shir are written alike in the Persian script, yet one means lion and the other means milk. Two things can look the same on the page and be nothing alike.
Rumi's worry is spiritual: people look at saints and prophets and say, they're just like us. But it works in a parking lot too. Before you decide what someone's going through, remember the parrot.

how: The grocer and the parrot is one of the Masnavi's short tales, and teachers use it to warn against judging others by oneself.

o: a gift to the poor, hoping for a blessing
a Persian pun where two words look alike
a comparison, measuring one thing by another

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: bald by choice, not by oil

s: it found its voice when a bald dervish passed, and made its wrong comparison.
sher and shir look alike written in Persian
one means lion, the other milk. same look, nothing alike.
the grocer was glad the parrot went quiet
he was heartbroken, pulled at his beard, and gave to the poor hoping it would speak.

games.q: you're the bald parrot. a man with a shining shaved head walks past the shop. what do you do?
o: say nothing; you've lost your voice.
call out: did you spill oil too?
ask him why his head is shaved.
games.why: the parrot cries out, did you spill oil too? everyone laughs at its comparison. same bald head, different story.

practice: Think of someone you've been judging lately, a relative, a neighbor, a person in the news, and notice the story you've told about why they are the way they are. Ask: is that their story, or mine?
Imagine two or three other reasons for the same bald head and hold them loosely; you don't need the real one, just a looser grip on your first guess.

wordCard.voice: Qiyas, the Persian word for analogy, the false comparison the parrot made between two different bald heads. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian, from Arabic: analogy, comparison. the parrot's wrong reasoning.

carryVoice: Your line: not the same bald. Lion and milk look alike on the page, too. Day one hundred seventy-six, done.
